# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Review: *Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations*

This is a strong follow-up. It answers most of the open questions from the earlier documents directly:
- **Longer horizon:** 24 months, with a randomised comparison.
- **Unrecorded work:** checked with a second hours measure from system logs.
- **Registered mediation test:** filed before outcomes were available.
- **Negative results reported openly:** the counter arm was ended at month 12, and three Halden organisations reverted.
- **Halden numbers treated as an upper bound,** not presented as general estimates.

Its rebuttals of the two earlier claims are largely justified:
- **Re-analysis ("entirely an artifact"):** a gain of 8.5% (CI 3.4 to 13.8) under the re-analysis's own recommended standards is hard to reconcile with that claim.
- **Meta-analysis ("no sign of decay"):** the four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. That confirms the concern I raised about that meta-analysis.

The arithmetic checks:
- Per-hour gains: 0.966/0.89 = +8.5% on logs; 0.966/0.88 = +9.8% on timesheets.
- Halden subset: 0.968/0.866 = +11.8%.
- Counter staffing: the 12% extra staff is consistent with the 9-month results. Restoring output requires about 1/(0.83 × 1.067) ≈ 1.13 times the staff.

The issues are mostly about how the decline is stated, what the log measure captures, contamination of the control group, and the strength of the mediation claim.

---

## 1. The Summary overstates the decline by comparing different measures

- **The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data."** But 12.5% is a timesheet figure. No log data exist for nine months.
- **Like for like, the decline is smaller.** On timesheets, the gain fell from 12.5% to 9.8%, a drop of about 22%. Mixing the two measures shows a drop of about 32%.
- **The body and Section 5 are correct** ("about a quarter"). Only the Summary needs fixing. Report both 24-month figures, labelled by measure.
- **The decline itself is uncertain.** The 9-month CI (6.9 to 18.4) and the 24-month CI (4.6 to 15.2) overlap heavily. The authors' wording ("consistent with some fading") is appropriately cautious. Keep it that way in the Summary too.
- **Two time points can't show whether the gain has levelled off.** "Declined but not disappeared" is accurate at 24 months. Avoid implying a plateau. That would repeat, in the opposite direction, the two-point extrapolation that the paper rightly criticises in the re-analysis.

## 2. What do system logs measure?

The logs are presented as a stricter measure of total hours. But they record active time on the case-management system. That probably excludes meetings, phone calls, reading, and other off-system work.

- **If so, logs measure time on case work, not total time worked.** Treated offices cut about 3.5 hours a week of meetings. A larger share of their remaining time would then be spent logged in, even with no change in unrecorded work.
- **That changes how two results read:**
  - "Log data show slightly more work than timesheets" could reflect time shifted from meetings to cases, not unclaimed hours.
  - In the mediation, meetings explaining output *per log-hour* implies a focus or fewer-interruptions mechanism, not simply freed-up time. That is a stronger and more specific claim, and worth stating as such.
- **Clarify:**
  - what "active log-in time" includes, and how idle time is handled;
  - whether pre-period log data were available, since the DiD needs a log baseline;
  - whether the log measure was added before or after the 24-month data were seen.

## 3. Contamination of the control group

Two control offices carried out a "meeting audit" in month 15 and cut recurring meetings.

- **This biases the treated-versus-control comparison toward zero.** If meeting cuts raise productivity, as the paper argues, the control group improved during the follow-up.
- **So part of the apparent decline from 12.5% to 9.8% may reflect control offices catching up,** not treated offices fading.
- **Report a sensitivity analysis.** For example:
  - exclude the two offices;
  - censor them from month 15;
  - or model the audit as a time-varying covariate.

  This could change the decline estimate noticeably.
- **The audit is also evidence of spread from treated to control offices.** Control managers knew about the trial and copied one of its features. This fits the "John Henry" concern raised at nine months, and should be named as such.

## 4. The mediation analysis: "confirms" is too strong

- **The independent units are 14 offices, not office-months.** "A larger sample of office-months" adds observations but not independent clusters. Only 7 offices received the treatment.
  - Explain how the CIs were computed, for example with a cluster bootstrap.
  - Apply the small-cluster correction I recommended at nine months, which still isn't mentioned.
  - A CI of 28–66% looks narrow for seven treated clusters.
- **The data are not an independent replication.** The analysis was registered at month 11, after the exploratory correlation (r = 0.71) had been seen. It uses the same offices, and probably the same early months. Registration rules out flexible analysis but not overfitting to these particular offices.
- **The causal assumptions are strong.** Meeting time was not randomised. Offices whose managers cut meetings may also have improved output by other means. The Limitations section acknowledges this, but the Summary's "confirms" doesn't reflect it.
- **The decomposition is ambiguous.**
  - Say whether the 47% and 18% shares were estimated jointly or one after another.
  - Say whether the two mediators are correlated, since fewer meetings could themselves reduce fatigue.
  - Give a CI for the "unexplained" 35%.
- **Suggested wording:** "A registered mediation analysis is consistent with meeting reduction accounting for roughly half of the per-hour gain, under the assumption of no unmeasured mediator–outcome confounding."

## 5. Outcomes still missing

- **Cost per case.** Case-processing timesheet hours fell by 12%, against 20% fewer scheduled hours. If the gap includes claimed overtime, paid at a premium, cost per case has probably risen. The paper costs out the counter arm (+9%) but not the case-processing arm, which is the one recommended for continuation.
- **Backlog and time to decision.** These are still unreported. Cases closed per FTE doesn't show whether queues grew or statutory deadlines were missed.
- **Quality.** Appeal overturn rates (3.2% v 3.0%) are still raw levels without a DiD estimate or CI.

## 6. Table 1 comparability

- **Sick days.** The 9-month figure of −29% was pooled across both strata in the original report. The 24-month −27% appears to cover case-processing only. Either restate the 9-month figure for case-processing alone or footnote the difference.
- **Resignations.** These are still raw treated-versus-control rates with no CI, from 14 offices.

## 7. Counter arm

- **Reporting the termination and its reasons is valuable.** It is the clearest real-world test of whether reduced hours work in coverage-bound settings.
- **Show how the 9% cost estimate was reached.** If labour were the only cost, 12% more staff would raise cost per contact by about 12%. Presumably non-labour costs make up the difference, so give the assumptions.
- **The month 10–12 waiting-time figures** (7.3 v 4.0 minutes) are now a treated-versus-control comparison, which is an improvement. But they are still not a DiD estimate with a CI.

## 8. Halden subset

The authors handle this honestly. Some refinements:
- **Selection runs through more than two stages.** The organisations had to:
  1. finish the pilot,
  2. submit output records,
  3. respond to follow-up (14 of 23),
  4. choose to continue.

  The non-response is also selective: 9 of 23 organisations declined.
- **Different subsets can't show anything about decay.** The 11.8% here and the 10.8% at six months (Varga & Holm's 17 organisations) come from different groups.
- **The marketing agency is informative.** It is nominally discretionary work, but it reverted over client deadlines. That complicates the meta-analysis's binary coding. Client responsiveness may act as a coverage constraint even in knowledge work. Worth drawing out.

## 9. Conflict of interest

- **The authors are evaluating disputes about their own work.** They include the original Varden team, whose meetings hypothesis is under dispute, and an author of the Halden working paper, which the re-analysis criticised.
- **The registered protocol and the frank reporting of negative results reduce this concern a good deal.** But a statement on the authors' roles would help.
- **Tone:** "since dismissed as post hoc" is a little adversarial. The re-analysis's scepticism was reasonable given the evidence at the time.

---

## Highest-value revisions

1. Fix the Summary's comparison across measures. Report both 24-month per-hour figures and the like-for-like decline (12.5% → 9.8%).
2. Define what log time captures, and reconsider the "more work than timesheets" interpretation and the mediation pathway in that light.
3. Run sensitivity analyses excluding or censoring the two control offices that audited their meetings.
4. Soften "confirms" for the mediation result. Report cluster-appropriate CIs, the method of decomposition, and how the mediators relate.
5. Add cost per case, backlog and time-to-decision outcomes for case-processing.
6. Make the sick-day figures comparable across the two time points.

The position the evidence now supports is narrower than either earlier claim. Under strong measurement standards, the per-hour gain in discretionary public-sector work is about 8–10% at two years, possibly fading slowly. In coverage-bound work it does not pay for itself. Meeting reduction is a plausible but not yet established contributor.

The open policy question the authors identify is whether reorganisation alone could capture much of the gain. Only a trial with a reorganisation-only arm can answer it, and it is the natural next study.
